newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Foote Cone & Belding says not shopping for scraps.
newsitem.headline: Foote Cone & Belding says not shopping for scraps.

text.p: Advertising agency Foote Cone & Belding (FCB) is not buying over-priced scraps left by its competitors despite being 15 years behind them in a fierce drive to go global, a senior executive told Reuters on Wednesday.
"We've been able to buy some of the few remaining jewels in the developing markets," Harry Reid, president of FCB International, said in an interview.
"Because we're late into it (globalisation), maybe 15 or 20 years behind a lot of our competitors, we're having to pay a little more than those guys did some years ago," Reid said.
"But we've bought some very good agencies," he added.

Reid, president of the international arm of U.S.-based FCB, a unit of True North Communications, was in Singapore to announce the acquisition of local agency Lloyd Martin which had billings of about Singapore $12 million in 1996.
The deal is the third such takeover staged by Western agencies in Singapore in the last five months.
In March, FCB lost out to UK-based Lowe Group in the race to buy the S$17 million-billing Monsoon agency.
In January, French agency Publicis bought 60 percent of Singapore agency Eureka which had a turnover of about S$30 million.
Earlier this month Publicis and True North ended a 10-year co-operation agreement the firms had hoped would build a formidable global alliance.
Reid said there was an element of catch-up in FCB's acquisition programme -- the financial details of which he declined to disclose -- but added it was almost complete.
An Indonesian deal would be announced in a few weeks and an operation in South Korea would complete the picture, he said.
Reid said the decision to go global had required "a total management, cultural shift" and that "the consequences of not doing this would have been dire".
Asia was vital to FCB's future plans said Reid, predicting that advertising spend in the region would leap to US$419 billion by 2020 from its 1995 level of US$73 billion.
FCB wants to generate about 25 percent of its income from Asia by 2000 from its 15 percent level, Reid said.
